blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ceftriaxone use with a penicillin-allergy history
stem: A client reports a penicillin allergy and is prescribed ceftriaxone. Which nursing interpretation is most accurate before administration?

options.A: Characterize the prior reaction because third-generation cephalosporin cross-reactivity is low, but high-risk IgE-mediated or severe delayed histories require additional evaluation.
options.B: Avoid every cephalosporin permanently because any reported penicillin allergy predicts the same reaction to all beta-lactam antibiotics.
options.C: Ignore the allergy history because ceftriaxone has no clinically relevant relationship to penicillins or other beta-lactam antibiotics.
options.D: Administer ceftriaxone without further review after any severe delayed beta-lactam reaction because delayed reactions do not affect future beta-lactam use.

rationale: CDC guidance states that third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone have low cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy and that evaluation begins with a thorough allergy history. High-risk IgE-mediated histories and severe non-IgE delayed reactions require a more cautious approach or specialist evaluation. Therefore A is correct. B is overly broad, C incorrectly dismisses beta-lactam relationships, and D conflicts with guidance for severe delayed reactions.
educational_objective: When ceftriaxone is considered in a client with a penicillin-allergy label, characterize the prior reaction and use reaction type and severity to guide risk assessment rather than assuming universal avoidance or universal safety.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines — Penicillin Allergy / Cross-Reactivity with Cephalosporins
source_version_date: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; current CDC guidance rechecked 2026-08-26
source_locator: Cross-Reactivity with Cephalosporins and Validating Penicillin or Another β-Lactam Antibiotic Allergy: third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone have <1% cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy; evaluation begins with a thorough history; high-risk histories require additional evaluation.
source_claim_supported: Third-generation cephalosporins have low cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy; allergy history and reaction severity/type guide further evaluation and treatment decisions.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: identify allergies and contraindications, review medication safety, and administer medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rebuilt all alternatives as complete allergy-risk interpretations of comparable length.
Preserved CDC's distinction between low third-generation cephalosporin cross-reactivity and high-risk allergy histories.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely reflects CDC guidance without converting low cross-reactivity into universal safety. No second defensible answer remains.
